fix(editor): use Prec.high for Emacs/Vim keymap extensions to fix keybinding conflicts

Emacs and Vim plugins use ViewPlugin DOM event handlers (keydown) to
intercept key events. When wrapped in Prec.low, these handlers run
after CodeMirror's built-in keymap handler (Prec.default), causing
conflicts with defaultKeymap Mac Ctrl-* bindings and completionKeymap
Ctrl-Space. This prevents Emacs keybindings like Ctrl-Y, Ctrl-W, and
Ctrl-SPC from being processed.

Change Emacs and Vim extensions to Prec.high so their DOM event
handlers run before the keymap handler, while keeping Prec.low for
VSCode and default keymaps that use keymap.of() and integrate with the
keymap handler directly.

Closes #10936

feat(editor): add Emacs markdown-mode keybindings with C-c C-s prefix

Register markdown formatting commands directly in the EmacsHandler using
its native key chain mechanism, following real Emacs markdown-mode conventions:

  C-c C-s b / B  → Bold (**text**)
  C-c C-s i / I  → Italic (*text*)
  C-c C-s c      → Code (`text`)
  C-c C-s s      → Strikethrough (~~text~~)
  C-c C-s p      → Pre/code block (```text```)

This approach:
- Uses 3-stroke key chains processed natively by the emacs plugin
- Avoids conflicts with Emacs navigation keys (C-b, C-f, etc.)
- Follows the Emacs convention of C-c prefix for mode-specific commands
- Keeps emacs-specific code in a dedicated module (emacs.ts)

In emacs mode, standard mod-* formatting shortcuts are excluded from
the editor shortcuts since they conflict with Emacs keybindings.

- Using toNonBlankStringOrUndefined() in proxyUriForCurrentType to normalize
  any falsy value (null, empty string) to undefined at the service layer
- Removing the erroneous nullish coalescing in getRespondUtil

fix(remark-drawio): prevent host CSS leaking into <foreignObject>

drawio sizes each diagram cell using user-agent default HTML metrics
and clips overflow via an inline max-height wrapper. When the host
page (e.g. GROWI's `.wiki`) applies descendant rules to elements like
`h1`, `p`, `li`, those rules cascade into HTML embedded inside SVG
`<foreignObject>` and inflate the rendered height, causing drawio to
clip the label content.

Add a defensive `all: revert` reset to common HTML elements inside
`<foreignObject>` so drawio cell labels render at UA-default metrics
regardless of host CSS, mirroring the existing
`.drawio-viewer * { box-sizing: content-box; }` defense.

Fixes #11052

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(remark-drawio): mark foreignObject reset as !important

Host selectors like `.wiki ol:not(.nav) li` outrank the scoped
`.drawio-viewer foreignObject li` reset on specificity (`:not(.nav)`
contributes a class-level weight), so `all: revert` was being
overridden and the cells continued to clip.

Defending foreignObject content is an adversarial cross-cutting
concern, so opt out of the specificity race with `!important` rather
than chasing host selectors. Mirrors the user-facing Custom CSS
workaround, which also relies on `!important` for the same reason.

Refs #11052

fix(app): set completedAt on all bulk export completion paths

The duplicate-reuse path (reuseDuplicateExportIfExists in
createPageSnapshotsAsync) marked a job as completed without setting
completedAt. The download-expiration cleanup query

normal compress-and-upload path), so every completion path expires
normally.

fix(core): use PCRE-safe regex escaping for MongoDB queries with non-ASCII whitespace

Node.js 24's RegExp.escape() escapes non-ASCII whitespace (code points
>= U+0100, e.g. U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE) into \uXXXX form. MongoDB's
PCRE2 engine does not support \u, so such patterns fail with error 51091,
breaking page creation and v5 page migration for paths containing those
characters.

Add escapeStringForMongoRegex() to @growi/core (escapes only regex
metacharacters and passes other characters through literally — equivalent
to escape-string-regexp v5, what GROWI used before the v7.5.0 refactor),
and use it at every call site where the escaped pattern is sent to MongoDB
(20 sites across page.ts, obsolete-page.js, page/index.ts, page-grant.ts,
users.js, openai.ts, generate-children-regexp.ts, remark-lsx list-pages).
In-process .test()/.replace() sites keep RegExp.escape().

Fixes #11235

fix(app): prevent bulk-export cleanup race on shared attachment

When the duplicate-reuse path produces multiple completed jobs that share a
single attachment, the download-expiration cleanup cron ran cleanUp() for
each job concurrently via Promise.allSettled. Each cleanUp called
attachmentService.removeAttachment for the same attachment, and the loser
of the race threw "Attachment not found" / GridFS "File not found". That
rejection excluded the losing job from the deleteMany() set, leaving a
zombie job record whose attachment ref was already gone. Every subsequent
cron tick re-attempted the same removal and produced the same error.

Two coordinated changes:

1. cron-side dedup: in deleteDownloadExpiredExportJobs, pick a single owner
   job per attachment from the expired batch and only run removeAttachment
   on the owner. Non-owner jobs still get their per-job resources cleaned
   up and the job record dropped by deleteMany, but they no longer race
   for the shared attachment.
2. removeAttachment idempotency: treat a missing attachment as a no-op
   instead of throwing, and swallow underlying deleteFile errors while
   still removing the metadata doc. This recovers existing zombie records
   on the next cron tick and adds defence-in-depth for any other concurrent
   caller (the attachment delete API and userSchema.deleteImage both
   pre-check or fire-and-forget, so the relaxed contract is safe for them).

fix(attachment): deny direct access to /uploads to prevent stored XSS

When the upload method is "Local", attachments are stored under
publicDir/uploads/** and were served directly by express.static(publicDir).
Direct access (e.g. /uploads/attachment/<file>) bypassed the /attachment and
/download routes, which apply authorization, Content-Disposition and
Content-Security-Policy headers — enabling stored XSS and access-control bypass.

Add a deny middleware that blanket-blocks the whole /uploads prefix and register
it before express.static so uploads are reachable only via the proxied routes.
Blocking the prefix (not individual subdirectories) ensures future storage
prefixes never silently re-open the hole.

installer, main and guest-mode sequentially in one job left only the last

redundantly in every chromium shard job, which both removes wasted runs and keeps

commands preserve the associativity of the selection head"). Bump both
@growi/editor and @growi/app from ^6.8.0 to ^6.10.3. Verified in a real
browser: selection now advances row by row across soft-wrapped lines.

rgb() without alpha channel — valid CSS Color Level 4 syntax — by
converting it to an invalid truncated hex value (e.g. rgb(0 0 255) → #00).

minification benefit is negligible compared to the risk of breaking
valid modern CSS syntax.

fix(page-bulk-export): render tables with borders in PDF export

Bulk-export PDF tables rendered without borders, header background, or cell
padding, while headings/blockquotes/code were styled correctly.

Root cause: `.wiki table` in _wiki.scss only sets font-size — it has no border
rules. GROWI's table borders come from the Bootstrap `table table-bordered`
classes that the web renderer adds via its add-class plugin. This spec's
pipeline emitted bare <table> elements (the earlier design assumed `.wiki table`
styled them, which is incorrect), so the .table/.table-bordered rules already
present in the precompiled CSS never applied.

Fix: reuse the web renderer's add-class rehype plugin (its only runtime dep,
hast-util-select, is ESM — loaded via dynamicImport, the same pattern as the
sanitize whitelist) to add `table table-bordered`, applied after rehype-sanitize
(static, trusted class values) and before rehype-stringify. No hand-written
table CSS; the design-system rules are reused as-is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(page-bulk-export): single-source the plugin pipeline; load by injection

Two responsibility/SRP improvements to the bulk-export markdown pipeline,
building on the table-rendering fix (which reused the web add-class plugin).

Single source of truth (plugin-set.ts):
- Declare add-class as a normal ADOPTED_PLUGINS entry (with specifier +
  exportName for its relative-path / named-export loading) instead of wiring it
  by hand in the renderer. The whole pipeline — npm plugins and the reused local
  add-class — is now one ordered declaration. This removes the positional
  special-case in buildProcessor and makes the parity test truthful (add-class
  moves from "intentionally excluded but actually reused" to a real adopted
  entry that matches its web import).

Loader does only loading (dependency injection):
- loadPlugins(baseDir, declarations) — the caller passes what to load; the loader
  no longer imports plugin-set, so it has a single responsibility and is unit
  testable with any declaration list. PluginDeclaration gains specifier/exportName
  so npm and reused-local plugins share one shape. Dropped the loader's module
  cache (redundant: the renderer's cachedProcessor already guarantees build-once),
  making the loader a side-effect-free function; added a clear error when a
  declared export is missing.

Spec docs (design/research/tasks) updated to match: add-class is adopted (not
excluded), loader is injection-based, and the research I-table premise is
corrected.

fix(revision-diff-api): correct changes-index keyset pagination (run loss + baseline shift)

While addressing kiro-review Finding 3 (perf), found and fixed two pre-existing
correctness bugs in the Changes Index pagination (both violate Req 3.3 / 4.3):

Bug A — runs dropped across pages. listChanges passed buildRuns output straight to
paginateRuns, but buildRuns emits runs in page-first-touch order, not the keyset order
(latestUpdatedAt, toRevisionId) paginateRuns requires. A run whose latest edit predated an
earlier-touched page's run was silently lost: page 1 emits the later run, sets the cursor
past the earlier run, and page 2's `> cursor` filter drops it. Fix: paginateRuns now sorts
its input into keyset order itself, so no caller can violate the precondition.

Bug B — baseline corruption for runs straddling the cursor. The cursor was applied in the
DB query, filtering out revisions at-or-before it. But a run's baseline (fromRevisionId) is
the revision immediately before the run's first edit and can predate the cursor; filtering
it out shifted a run's page-creation baseline (null) to the user's own intermediate
revision, losing diff content. Fix: do NOT apply the cursor in the DB query — recompute
runs over the full window each page and apply the cursor in-memory in paginateRuns, so
baselines are always computed from full history.

Finding 3 (perf) — bound the distinct page-scan by max(since, cursor.createdAt): a page
whose latest own-edit predates the cursor cannot contribute a later run, so it is excluded
from the window scan (reduces forward-pagination cost). The per-page recompute over the
window is inherent to correct baselines; documented in design.md, mitigated by since-based
incremental sync. The concurrent-mid-pagination edge (a run extended between page fetches
reappears as a superset entry, not a duplicate/lost one) is also documented.

Tests (TDD red→green): unit test that paginateRuns sorts unsorted input; integ tests that a
run is not dropped on cross-page time interleave and that a page-creation baseline survives
a pagination boundary. Full feature suite green (68), tsgo --noEmit + biome pass.

fix(app): prevent blank screen when Next.js falls back to the error page

GrowiApp.getInitialProps unconditionally called getLocaleAtServerSide,
which destructures req without a null check. Next.js re-invokes _app's
getInitialProps on the client (with a ctx that omits req/res) when it
falls back to rendering the built-in error page after an uncaught
client-side render exception. That made the fallback render throw too,
so neither the original page nor the error page could render, leaving
a blank screen instead of Next's error page.

Add getUserLocaleForApp, which returns undefined when req is missing
instead of crashing, and skip the <html lang> update in that case.

Fixes #11422

fix(app): prevent PageSelectModal infinite render loop (#11422)

The scroller <div> that owns the callback ref setting `scrollerElem`
lived INSIDE the <Suspense> boundary. When ItemsTree suspends
(useSWRxRootPage with suspense on a cold cache), React hides the
boundary's primary content and detaches that ref (calls it with null),
resetting `scrollerElem`. That unmounts ItemsTree, the content reveals,
the ref re-attaches (sets `scrollerElem` again), ItemsTree suspends
again — an unbounded render loop ("Maximum update depth exceeded").
It only reproduced on a cold SWR cache (first open), which is why
component tests with synchronous data did not catch it.

Move the ref-bearing scroller <div> OUTSIDE <Suspense> so it is never
hidden/detached; only ItemsTree stays inside the boundary. Add a
regression test that suspends ItemsTree via a thrown promise and
asserts the tree renders without the loop.

feat(esm-migration): capture WebSocket authz matrix baseline (task 0.3.2)

Add apps/app/tools/capture-ws-authz.ts + authz-matrix/ws-fixtures.ts that
boot Crowi with a real HTTP listener on 127.0.0.1:13000, seed a test user
and two pages (GRANT_PUBLIC viewable / GRANT_OWNER unviewable), log in to
/_api/v3/login to extract a real express-session cookie, and open real
WebSocket upgrades against /yjs/<pageId> and socket.io-client connects
against the default / and /admin namespaces.

Yjs captures 3 cases:
- no-session @ unviewable page -> 401 (null-user ACL reject)
- session + unviewable page    -> 403 (isAccessiblePageByViewer=false)
- session + viewable page      -> 101 + sync frame received
Socket.io captures 3 cases (session-unviewable substituted with
session-nonadmin-admin-ns because socket.io has no per-page ACL at
connect time; substitution documented in baseline notes):
- no-session                    -> rejected (loginRequired)
- non-admin on /admin ns        -> rejected (adminRequired)
- non-admin on /                -> connected

Baseline committed: .kiro/specs/esm-migration/ws-authz-baseline.json.
Phase 3.8.d will diff this against the ESM-built server output.

feat(growi-vault): implement Stage 2 rename and grant-change propagation

Extend GROWI core PageService event payloads and wire vault subscribers
to propagate parent page rename and bulk grant changes to vault without
requiring a manual bootstrap re-run.

GROWI core changes:
- pageEvent.emit('rename') now carries { page, oldPath, newPath, user }
  at both single-page rename call sites
- pageEvent.emit('updateMany') now carries a 4th arg
  { oldPagePathPrefix, newPagePathPrefix } from both renameDescendants
  call sites — existing subscribers that only read (pages, user) are
  unaffected
- updateChildPagesGrant emits new event 'descendantsGrantChanged'
  { affectedPages, user } after Page.bulkWrite(), carrying per-page old/new
  grant snapshots so subscribers can compute namespace deltas

Vault subscriber changes (server/index.ts):
- 'rename': compute page namespaces → dispatch rename-prefix per namespace
- 'updateMany': when prefix extras are present (Stage 2), de-dup affected
  namespaces and dispatch a single rename-prefix instruction; fall back to
  per-page upsert for legacy emits without extras (Stage 1 path preserved)
- 'descendantsGrantChanged': translate each affected page into a per-page
  acl-change event routed through the existing dispatcher (remove from
  previous namespaces + upsert to current namespaces)
- 'syncDescendantsUpdate': demote WARN to debug — now handled by updateMany
- grant-change-prefix op not used: its payload has no path scope, so it
  cannot express a partial subtree grant change; acl-change path is correct

Tests: 8 new cases in server/index.spec.ts covering the three new
subscribers (14 total; all pass). page.integ.ts (35 tests) passes with
no regressions from the emit payload additions.

     ephemeral port pointing at the test's mongo-memory-server. Shares a
     fresh internal-secret with the apps/app side via env.
  2. seed.ts — register the Crowi-bound mongoose models with a stub Crowi
     (idempotent across files when isolate=false), seed admin + member
     users, generate two PATs via AccessToken.generateToken (same path the
     production auth middleware exercises), and seed the deterministic
     fixture pages from fixture-contract.ts.
  3. express-mount.ts — bind the vault gateway router on an ephemeral local
     port so the integ tests exercise the real HTTP path → vault-manager
     RPC + git pack-data.
  4. provision.ts — orchestrate the above, run the vault bootstrapper, wait
     for vault-manager to drain the instructions outbox so namespaces are
     materialised before tests run.
  5. fixture-handle.ts — expose dispatcher + bootstrapper handles so the
     coalesce/null-revision tests can exercise them directly without
     adding test-only HTTP endpoints to production code.
  6. index.ts — vitest setupFile wiring beforeAll/afterAll.

emits remove(oldPath) + upsert(newPath) per namespace, correctly moving
the page's own blob. Descendant subtree relocation is unchanged and still
handled by the 'updateMany' -> rename-prefix path. Grant is unchanged by a
rename, so old/new paths share the same namespace set.

fix(growi-vault-manager): serialize change-stream instruction processing

The post-drain change-stream listener was an async EventEmitter handler;
Node does not await async listeners, so consecutive instructions ran
applyInstruction concurrently. commitAndUpdateRef performs an unguarded
read-parent -> writeCommit -> updateRef (no compare-and-swap), so two
instructions on the same namespace applied concurrently both read the same
parent commit and the last updateRef wins, losing one update.

This is what defeated the single-page rename fix end-to-end: onPageRenamed
emits remove(oldPath) + upsert(newPath) on the same namespace; processed
concurrently, the remove was clobbered by the upsert and the old file
stayed orphaned in the clone.

Chain each change event synchronously onto the single pipeline promise so
instructions are applied one at a time, in arrival order, after the startup
drain — mirroring the already-sequential drain path.

- watcher: extract handleChangeEvent; chain onto pipelinePromise at arrival
- watcher spec: regression test asserting no overlapping applyInstruction
- gateway clone-e2e: end-to-end regression — create -> rename -> clone
  asserts old file removed, new file present with original body

test(growi-vault): fix race in resilience-flow force-bootstrap scenario

Scenario (f) fires the force bootstrap as a background task via
initOnStartup() and polled getStatus() until bootstrapState became 'done',
then asserted the 'vault.resilience.bootstrap-completed' audit event. The
runner writes state='done' to the DB *before* emitting that audit event
(state is the source of truth; the audit call is awaited afterwards), so the
poll could observe 'done' and assert before the event was recorded — a race
that surfaced under slower CI I/O (the audit array held only 2 events).
Confirmed deterministically by widening the window between the 'done' write
and the audit emission.

Wait for the completion audit event as part of the settle condition on the
success path (failure still settles at 'failed'). Production code is
unchanged; the other scenarios await bootstrap() directly and are unaffected.

test(growi-vault-manager): isolate integ tests per worker via in-process server

The three *.integ.ts files ran against a single shared vault-manager whose
watcher applies every instruction through one global serialized pipeline
(commit c25dc61b). Vitest runs test files in parallel, so all files' inserts
queued behind one another and the tightest-deadline test (rename-prefix, 10s)
timed out in CI — while every instruction still eventually processed
(processedAt set, lastError 0, no dead-letter): a contention problem, not a
logic bug.

Isolate per worker instead of disabling parallelism (mirrors apps/app's
per-worker DB isolation):

- extract index.ts bootstrap into server-runtime.ts startServer(); index.ts
  becomes a thin entrypoint (production behavior unchanged)
- new setupFile boots one in-process vault-manager per worker, bound to a
  per-worker DB (growi-vault-integ-<workerId>), bare repo, and port; torn
  down with server.stop() — no child-process spawn/kill
- integ connectMongo/disconnectMongo reuse the setup's connection
- ci-vault.yml: drop the start/wait/stop-server steps; just provide MongoDB
  and run test:integ (mirrors ci-app.yml)

Verified locally: typecheck/build green, unit 181 green (setupFile is a no-op
without RUN_VAULT_INTEG), parallel integ 16/16 green on two consecutive runs.

refactor(esm-migration): 起動失敗の出力を stderr.write から console.error (biome-ignore) へ

process.stderr.write は no-console ルールを機械的に回避するだけで、ルールの趣旨
(ログは pino に一本化) を曖昧にしていた。本質は「pino の Worker-thread transport
は非同期で、強制 process.exit(1) の前に flush できないため、致命的な起動エラーが
消える」こと。強制 exit 直前の last-gasp 出力は同期 console が本来の正しい道具
であり、console が本当に必要なケース。よって stderr.write での言い換えをやめ、
理由を明記した biome-ignore 付き console.error に変更。pino raw-JSON モード
(transport 無し・同期 flush) 向けに logger.error も併置。

feat(suggest-path-evaluator): align granularity and add near-miss / new-path verdicts

Refine the evaluator to match suggest-path's actual contract and the failure
modes seen in #184610 measurements:

- Granularity: Claude now produces a parent path to save UNDER (same units as
  suggest-path), not a full path for a hypothetical new page. Comparisons are
  parent-vs-parent so they can no longer be off by one level.
- Sibling test: one general rule (where would the document sit as a sibling? its
  siblings' parent is the answer) covers both 'an existing topic page' and
  'only same-kind records exist', avoiding both over-nesting and stepping up.

  wrong depth) / miss, so the dominant parent-stop failure gets its own bucket.

  new path is the correct behavior (hit-new / near-miss-new / miss-misfiled),
  not an automatic miss.

fix(vault-manager): run container as non-root via privilege-drop entrypoint; adopt corepack

The release container ran the app as root and installed pnpm via a wget
standalone script. Two changes:

- Non-root: add docker/docker-entrypoint.ts (run via Node 24 type stripping)
  that creates and chowns the bare repo on the shared /data volume as root,
  then drops to the node user (uid/gid 1000) via process.setgid/setuid before
  exec'ing the app. This aligns vault-manager and apps/app on a single uid so
  they can share /data (Requirement 10.3); no gosu/setpriv binary is needed.
  The entrypoint lives in docker/ (not src/) so it stays out of the dist/
  artifact, and is copied raw to /docker-entrypoint.ts in the image.
- pnpm: activate via `corepack enable` (version pinned by the workspace
  packageManager field), matching apps/app. Build stages run on the official
  node:24-bookworm image because corepack's pnpm shim is not executable on the
  DHI dev image; only the release stage uses DHI dev (for the git binary).

Verified: 9 new unit tests, biome, typecheck, and a full docker build + runtime
check (both processes run as uid 1000, repo dir owned by 1000, entrypoint not
present in dist).

feat(suggest-path-agentic): rebuild instructions around peer-default placement (#185213)

Replace the "always descend to the MOST SPECIFIC page" rule (A-9..A-12) with a
peer-vs-sub-detail judgement. Because suggestPath returns the PARENT a document
is saved UNDER, a self-contained document is a sibling of related pages, not a
child of one of them: the right answer is usually the shared category, not the
matching leaf page. The descend-strong rule optimized for an answer key that had
silently drifted to "hit the real page", which pushed the true (parent) answer
out of the top rank.

The new instructions default to PEER (propose the category the related pages sit
in) and descend only when the document is genuinely a sub-detail of one specific
page.

Measured against parent answers (the document's real page's parent):
- body input, 180 calls: parent-as-rank-1 18.3% -> 73.3%, exact-parent
  58.9% -> 88.9%, MRR 0.338 -> 0.796
- spec input (spec6), 60 calls: parent-as-rank-1 3.3% -> 65.0%, exact-parent
  68.3% -> 91.7%, MRR 0.273 -> 0.760

(B) startsWith (whether the correct parent subtree appears at all) stays roughly
flat (99.4% -> 96.1% body), confirming retrieval was already adequate and only
the ranking needed fixing.

feat(suggest-path-evaluator): add body-swap self-consistency gate

Add a self-consistency gate to the evaluator so it can detect when the
judgment for one document was mistakenly formed from another document's
content (a "body swap"). This failure surfaced during a full blind 66-case
run where two adjacent cases had their reasoning swapped; previously it was
only caught because the verdicts disagreed with a human answer key, which
breaks the skill's "no human ground truth" premise.

The gate works on the body alone:
- step 3 now produces a one-line body digest (subject + key terms taken
  verbatim from the body) and verifies every key term appears in the body
  it claims to describe; a mismatch means a different document was
  summarized, so the answer is discarded and step 3 re-run.
- the report structure carries the digest as evidence.
- batch mode makes the gate mandatory (parallel sub-agents are where swaps
  happen) and defines a closed self-repair loop: reconcile every digest
  against its body, quarantine failures, re-judge, re-reconcile, and only
  then aggregate.

Add scripts/reconcile-digests.py implementing the reconciliation as a
deterministic string check (LLM re-judging could drift the same way the
original mistake did). It splits compound terms on separators to tolerate
formatting differences, exits non-zero on any suspected swap to block
aggregation, and lists quarantined ids. Verified on the 66-case dataset:
all 66 pass, and an injected swap is correctly flagged and quarantined.

Miss-rate tracing showed the agent's search-query generation, not the
ReAct loop or ES retrieval, is the root cause of misses: it rephrases the
document's topic across the whole budget and never varies the axis, so it
fails to surface shelves grouped by document KIND or reachable only via a
path slug.

Rebuild Step 3 around how an expert greps an unfamiliar codebase, derived
from a blind exemplar agent that reached the correct page in 4/5 prior
miss cases using the same ES search path:

- Frame search as guessing the literal words the target shelf and its
  pages contain, not restating the topic.
- Search on the document's KIND, not only its topic; shelves are usually
  grouped by kind.
- Query literal path slugs: a page's PATH is often a short identifier in a
  different language than its prose (an English/ASCII slug under a Japanese
  body), and search weights the path highest.
- Follow the terrain: read the paths the hits reveal and drill into the
  shared segment with prefix:, instead of rephrasing the topic.

before proposing it.

fix(mastra): cap client-supplied model id length (defensive)

The per-request `modelId` (POST /mastra/message) and the persisted
`aiChatSelectedModelId` (PUT /user-ui-settings) were validated as
`.isString()` with no length bound. Both are untrusted client input:
`modelId` is logged verbatim by resolveEffectiveModelId on every
out-of-allowlist request, and `aiChatSelectedModelId` is stored in
UserUISettings. An authenticated client could send an unbounded string to
bloat logs per request or bloat the persisted document. Neither bypasses the
allow-list (both are rounded server-side), so this is purely a defensive
hardening.

Add a shared MAX_MODEL_ID_LENGTH (256 — far above any real model id / Azure
deployment name) in the mastra interfaces and apply `.isLength({ max })` to
both validators. Lift the user-ui-settings PUT validator to an exported
module-scope const (validatorForPutUserUISettings) so its contract is
unit-testable directly, mirroring the put-ai-settings convention.

fix(build): pin @babel/core so next symlinks survive pnpm deploy --prod

next@16 declares @babel/core as an optional peer, and pnpm bakes the resolved
peer version into next's (and next-i18next's, which embeds next's)
.next/node_modules/<pkg>-<hash> virtual-store path. The full dev install dedupes
@babel/core to 7.29.7, but `pnpm deploy --prod` (assemble-prod.sh) re-resolved
the prod-only graph to 7.29.0 — a different .pnpm dir name — so the symlinks
Turbopack baked at build time dangled in the prod tarball and
check-next-symlinks.sh failed on `next` and `next-i18next`.

ALLOWED_BROKEN would be the wrong fix: the SSR server bundle require()s the
hashed name at render time (`require("next-...hash.../error.js")`), so a broken
symlink crashes production with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND even though CI would pass.

Pin @babel/core to a single patch (7.29.7, already what the dev install uses) in
pnpm-workspace.yaml overrides so dev and prod resolve identically. babel is an
unused optional peer here (GROWI builds with Turbopack/SWC), so the pin is safe.

Verified non-destructively: fresh build + `pnpm deploy --prod` → 144/148
.next/node_modules symlinks resolve; the only 4 broken are the existing
ALLOWED_BROKEN entries (fslightbox-react, socket.io-client, @emoji-mart/react,
@emoji-mart/data). Also documents this peer-hash-drift case (Step 3c) in the
fix-broken-next-symlinks skill and package-dependencies rule.

refactor(revision-diff): drop redundant index migration; build via schema autoIndex

The { author: 1, createdAt: -1 } index on revisions is already declared in
the schema (revision.ts), so Mongoose autoIndex builds it at startup like
every other GROWI index. The dedicated migrate-mongo migration was redundant
and, unlike autoIndex, blocked startup and was fatal on failure. For shared
MongoDB deployments (GROWI.cloud) the index is pre-created via ops before
upgrade, so the startup-time build becomes an idempotent no-op.

fix(activities-prisma-migration): normalize target/event/userId in updateByParameters

Prisma's update() cannot serialize a Mongoose Document or bare ObjectId the
way Mongoose's own findOneAndUpdate auto-cast them, so callers such as
update-page.ts's PAGE_UPDATE settle path (target: updatedPage) and the
contribution-graph orchestration (target: pageId) silently failed to settle
the activity, leaving it stuck at UNSETTLED. Mirrors createByParameters's
existing normalizeToId for the update path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(activities-prisma-migration): wrap ObjectId/Date in Extended JSON for aggregateRaw

A raw mongoose.Types.ObjectId or Date placed directly in an aggregateRaw
$match serializes to a plain JSON string/ISO string, which does not match
a stored BSON ObjectId/Date field -- the query silently returned zero
results. This broke GET /api/v3/user-activities (always empty) and the
contribution-graph migration (never produced contributions).

Adds toRawObjectId/toRawDate (MongoDB Extended JSON $oid/$date) and applies
them in both aggregateRaw pipeline builders. Also extracts user-activities.ts's
inline pipeline into an exported, unit-tested buildUserActivityPipeline
(dropping the `as unknown as Record<string, unknown>[]` cast), and fixes
aggregate-user-activities.integ.ts, which had drifted from production by
maintaining its own stale copy of the pipeline builder instead of importing it.

Also fixes utils/prisma.ts's paginateLogic to coerce offset/limit to numbers:
Express query params arrive as strings even after express-validator's
`.isInt()` (which validates but does not sanitize), and Prisma's skip/take
reject strings with PrismaClientValidationError, unlike mongoose-paginate-v2
which coerced internally. This broke the audit-log list endpoint for any
request carrying its normal string query params.

refactor(activities-prisma-migration): validate aggregateRaw shape instead of blind casts

aggregateUserActivities / aggregateContributions cast an unvalidated
aggregateRaw result straight to the expected type at every step
(normalizeAggregateRaw(...) as X[], facetDoc.docs as unknown[] ?? [], ...).
A structurally wrong pipeline result (e.g. a broken $facet, a renamed key)
produced an empty-looking value that type-checked fine and was
indistinguishable from a genuine "no matching activities" outcome -- this
is exactly the failure mode that let the toRawObjectId/toRawDate
regressions ship undetected.

Adds assertIsArray (an `asserts` type guard) and applies it at each
structural boundary of the raw result -- the outer array, the $facet
document, and its docs/totalCount arrays -- so a shape mismatch now throws
with the offending path instead of silently flowing through. Only the
terminal "trust the array elements match the interface" cast remains,
matching the boundary-cast idiom already used elsewhere in this codebase
(e.g. apiv3/activity.ts's paginateResult.docs cast).

fix(@growi/app): ship Prisma query engine for production SSR

The production `/` page 500s with `PrismaClientInitializationError: Prisma
Client could not locate the Query Engine for runtime "debian-openssl-3.0.x"`.
The Next.js SSR bundle resolves the native engine at
`process.cwd()/src/generated/prisma/`, but neither the Docker release nor the
CI tarball ships `src/` — only `dist/generated/prisma` (the Express consumer)
gets the engine, via bin/postbuild-server.ts.

- prisma/schema.prisma: declare binaryTargets (native + debian-openssl-3.0.x +
  linux-arm64-openssl-3.0.x) so the required engines are always generated
  regardless of build host, and the turbo `prisma:generate` cache is
  architecture-safe.
- docker/Dockerfile & reusable-app-prod.yml: ship the engine binaries to
  apps/app/src/generated/prisma so the SSR consumer can locate them.

Latent since Prisma was introduced; activated by 554fa9311a (bookmark model ->
Prisma), which put prisma.bookmarks.count() on the page-view getServerSideProps
path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(@growi/app): stage Prisma engine in /tmp/prisma-engines for SSR

The previous approach (shipping the engine to src/generated/prisma) did not work.
@prisma/client's resolveEnginePath searches only:
  [dirname, resolve(dirname,".."), generator.output.value,
   resolve(dirname,"../../../.prisma/client"), "/tmp/prisma-engines", cwd]
In the Turbopack-bundled SSR chunk, every entry except the hardcoded literal
"/tmp/prisma-engines" is rewritten or absent at runtime (hence the prod error
listing /ROOT/... and /opt/apps/app/... build paths). src/generated/prisma is
not in the list at all, so the earlier copy never helped.

Copy the engines (shipped in dist/generated/prisma via postbuild-server.ts) into
/tmp/prisma-engines at container start (as root, world-readable for the node
user), so the SSR consumer resolves the engine matching the runtime platform.
Revert the ineffective src/generated/prisma copies in Dockerfile /
reusable-app-prod.yml. binaryTargets stays: it guarantees both engines exist in
dist regardless of build host / turbo cache architecture.

Verified faithfully: with the engine absent from the baked output path
(reproducing prod) prisma.bookmarks.count() fails with the exact
"could not locate the Query Engine" error; placing it in /tmp/prisma-engines
makes the identical call succeed against MongoDB.

fix(editor): dedupe server-side yjs to a single ESM instance to stop collaborative draft revert

On dev/8.0.x the collaborative editor reverted typed text to the just-loaded state a
few seconds after typing — on the 2nd editing session of any page that already had a
persisted Yjs draft (single user, no further action needed; preview-verified).

Root cause: yjs was loaded as TWO module instances on the server. yjs ships dual builds
and its exports split `import` -> dist/yjs.mjs (ESM) and `require` -> dist/yjs.cjs (CJS).
After the ESM migration, apps/app imports yjs as ESM (yjs.mjs) while the CJS-only
`y-websocket/bin/utils` does `require('yjs')` -> yjs.cjs. Yjs relies on instanceof/type
identity, so the WSSharedDoc created by y-websocket (yjs.cjs) is foreign to the app's
yjs.mjs. Session 1 (fresh doc) works; on session 2 the persisted doc is reconstructed
in bindState and the client's edits no longer merge into the live server doc, so the
server's periodic resync reverts the client. Confirmed at runtime:
`liveYdoc instanceof Y.Doc === false`, and client edits did not grow the server's
codemirror text. (v7.5.6 was all-CJS -> single instance, hence unaffected.)

Patch yjs's package exports so `require` also resolves to dist/yjs.mjs (via Node's
require(esm)), unifying every consumer to the single ESM instance. `import`/`module`
are unchanged, so the client (already single-instance ESM) is untouched. y-websocket v3
dropped bin/utils and its successor @y/websocket-server requires yjs v14, so a package
upgrade is not a drop-in fix while we remain on yjs 13.

Verified on the dev server: server boots (require(esm) OK), `liveYdoc instanceof Y.Doc
=== true`, client edits merge into the server doc, and a 2-session edit persists with
no revert.

perf(docker): add opt-in jemalloc allocator via JEMALLOC_ENABLED

Under GROWI's load profile, glibc malloc retains hundreds of MiB of freed
memory in its main arena ([heap] segment) — fragmentation prevents
trimming, so the container's working set stays inflated long after load
has drained. Measured with the memory-profiler scenario (production dist,
100 Yjs sessions + page load, 300s idles): drain-phase retention drops
from +468 MiB (glibc) to +142 MiB with jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD (-70%),
while MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 has no effect (+456) and a pinned
MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_ recovers only ~50 MiB.

Ship libjemalloc2 in the image (copied from a debian:13 stage — the
hardened runtime has no package manager) and let operators opt in with
JEMALLOC_ENABLED=true. The entrypoint preloads it for the app process
only; a missing library logs an error and falls back to glibc malloc
without blocking boot.

fix(mastra): return snippets from full-text-search-tool via formatSearchResult

The full-text search tool read only `_highlight.body`, the highlight key ES
emits solely for phrase (`"..."`) matches. Plain keyword matches land on
`body.ja` / `body.en` (and `comments.*`), so the snippet was dropped for
almost every search. It also bypassed the `canShowSnippet` visibility gate,
so surfacing the snippet naively would have leaked body fragments of pages
the caller cannot view.

Route the raw result through `SearchService.formatSearchResult` — the same
path `/_api/search` uses — which owns both the highlight-key fallback and the
grant gate, then project to `{ pageId, pagePath, snippet }`. Widen
`formatSearchResult` / `checkIsFormattable` `delegatorName` to `string | null`
to match `searchKeyword`'s return type. Also drop leftover `console.log`s.

feat(activity): add POST /_api/v3/activity/list carrying the filter in the body

The audit-log list is fetched via GET /_api/v3/activity with the searchFilter
JSON-encoded into the query string. Because every available action is selected
by default, the URL lists them all; for large action-group configs (~145
actions) the URL-encoded query approaches ~9KB and can exceed common proxy
header limits (e.g. nginx's default 8KB).

Add POST /_api/v3/activity/list, which takes limit / offset / searchFilter in
the request body so the filter never touches the URL. The GET route is kept
unchanged for API/PAT backward compatibility; both share one implementation
extracted to fetch-activity-list.ts (resolveActivityListWhere + paginate),
so filter/serialize behaviour cannot drift between the two.

Offset note: GET's `offset || 1` quirk only skips on an ABSENT offset because a
query string turns an explicit 0 into the truthy "0". The POST body carries a
real numeric 0, so the POST route treats offset as a plain 0-based skip count
(0 → no skip) to keep page 1 showing the newest record.

fix(admin): derive export archive list from server state via SWR

The admin "Export Archive Data" list showed duplicate rows, and deleting
one duplicate removed both (#11509).

The cause was architectural, not a missing dedup guard. The archive list
is server state derived from the filesystem (GET /export/status), but the
client kept a hand-maintained mirror of it: it appended the
admin:onTerminateForExport payload to local state and filtered by
fileName on delete. When the completion event was processed more than
once (the effect re-subscribing as the admin socket transitions from null
to connected, combined with React StrictMode's double effect), the same
archive was appended twice; because delete filters by fileName, removing
either row removed both.

Rather than guard the append, treat the list as server state:
- read zipFileStats through SWR (useSWRxExportStatus), the single source
  of truth, so the rendered list always equals the server's filesystem;
- on completion and after delete, revalidate with mutate() instead of
  mutating local state -- mutate() is idempotent, so a doubled event can
  never produce duplicate rows;
- guard the null stat that a broken zip emits so the listener no longer
  throws while dereferencing it.

Transient progress state (isExporting / progressList / isZipping) stays
socket-driven; only the persisted list moves to SWR.

Adds ExportArchiveDataPage.spec.tsx covering the #11509 duplicate-row
contract, the null-payload crash, and delete re-syncing from the server.

Closes #11509

The PAGE_UPDATE activity was emitted from postAction AFTER res.apiv3(), behind

fix(remark-drawio): keep multi-page diagram on its page during navigation

Clicking the viewer's page-navigation arrow resizes the diagram vertically,
which the ResizeObserver treated as a container resize and reacted to by
recreating the GraphViewer from scratch. The recreated viewer always starts on
the first page, while the previous instance's toolbar (appended to document.body
on hover) kept showing the target page number — so the diagram snapped back to
page 1 while the control still read e.g. "2 / 2".

The outer .drawio-viewer is a block element whose width is fixed by the
surrounding layout, so page navigation only changes its height. Gate the
re-render on width: height-only changes (page navigation) no longer recreate the
viewer, while genuine layout changes (window/pane resize) still do. The decision
is extracted as the pure function shouldRerenderOnResize with unit tests.

Known limitation: if navigating to a taller page makes a page-level scrollbar
appear (space-taking scrollbars only), the content width shrinks by a few px and
triggers one re-render that resets to page 1; it self-heals on the next click.

ci(release-subpackages): gate the snapshot job on planned releases

The snapshot job started whenever any changeset file existed. With only a
changeset for an ignored package left, 'changeset version --snapshot' bumped
nothing, so 'changeset publish --snapshot --tag next' pushed the plain versions
already in the tree to npm under the 'next' dist-tag - which is how
@growi/core@2.5.0 and @growi/pluginkit@1.2.7 ended up published as 'next' while
'latest' stayed on the previous release.

Count the packages the release plan actually bumps instead. Ignored packages
appear in .releases as dependents with type "none", so they are filtered out.

fix(vault): clear the resume cursor when a rebuild starts

A force wipe re-seeds the vault from the first page, so a cursor left over
from an earlier run is not a valid resume point. The wipe path only ignored
the cursor in memory (`resumeCursor`) and left the persisted field alone,
and the persisted field is not overwritten until the first page is streamed.

A wipe that died in that window therefore left the previous run's cursor
behind. The next resume queried `_id > <old cursor>` against a repository the
wipe had already emptied, skipped every page below it, and still satisfied
the completeness check (which only asks whether the cursor reached the
snapshot max id) — reporting `done` for a vault with most of its pages
missing.

Clear bootstrapCursor in the same update that transitions the state to
running, so the crash window cannot leave a stale resume point behind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(vault): recover a bootstrap whose runner is gone

bootstrapState 'running' / 'verifying' only move forward while the process
that owns the run is alive, so a mid-bootstrap crash froze them for good: the
gateway answered 503 for every clone, and all three ways out were closed.

- the startup normalization only rescued a 'running' document whose
  bootstrapInstanceId was null, but the id is written at the start of every
  run and therefore survives the crash — the check skipped exactly the
  documents it should have rescued;
- the heartbeat-based resume is only evaluated when VAULT_BOOTSTRAP_ON_START
  is 'true' or 'force', and it defaults to 'false';
- the admin "Rebuild Vault" button is disabled whenever the state looks
  in-flight, so an operator could not restart the run either.

Decide liveness from the heartbeat instead, in one shared pure predicate
(isStaleBootstrapRunner) that both the startup normalization and the status
API apply, so the two cannot disagree about what an abandoned run is. The
startup path now covers 'verifying' as well — the heartbeat keeps ticking
through the completeness check, and the trigger resolver always skips
'verifying', which made it an even deeper dead end than 'running'.

GET /_api/v3/vault/status reports the verdict as isStaleRunner (computed
server-side: the staleness threshold is server config, not something a
client should re-derive from a timestamp), and the admin UI enables Rebuild
Vault for an abandoned run, with a notice explaining why a destructive
button is available next to a "running" status.

The resume cursor is deliberately preserved when normalizing: for a non-wipe
run it is still a valid resume point, and a wipe clears it when it starts.

fix(vault-manager): keep tree entry names within the 255-byte filesystem limit

ext4 and APFS reject a path component longer than 255 bytes, and git aborts the
whole checkout on the first rejected file — so a single page whose title reaches
85 Japanese characters made the entire clone unusable.

VaultTreeNormalizer now shortens such names and gives them the same __<hash8>
suffix it already uses for case collisions. The budget is applied to the final
name, suffix included, because the 10-byte suffix can by itself push a name that
fits over the limit. Names that already fit are returned byte-for-byte
unchanged, so existing clones see no rename churn.

fix(vault): reject wants for objects outside the requester's view

GIT_NAMESPACE scopes ref advertisement, not the object store, and git's
reachability check for an unadvertised want assumes the want is a commit.
Blobs and trees were therefore served for any OID present in the shared
object database, whatever view the client authenticated into - including
a blob no ref reaches at all. One tree yields the file names plus the
child OIDs, so a whole private subtree could be walked from a single ID.
gitnamespaces(7) says namespaces are not effective for read access
control, so this cannot be fixed by configuration.

GitProxyController now authorises the request before upload-pack runs:

- parseWantSection (vault-pkt-line.ts) reads the pkt-lines at the head of
  the body up to the flush packet and returns the requested OIDs. Pure,
  so it is tested without a stream or a git process.
- peekWantSection (vault-want-guard.ts) does that over the request
  stream. It pauses rather than iterating, because consuming the stream
  with `for await` closes it and drops the negotiation that follows the
  want section, which leaves upload-pack waiting on input forever - that
  hang showed up in a prototype before this landed. The peeked bytes are
  replayed through the spawner's new stdinPrefix so upload-pack still
  gets a byte-identical body.
- findWantsOutsideView runs `git merge-base --is-ancestor <want> <view
  ref>` per want. That single command denies non-commits, other views'
  commits, missing objects and a missing view ref alike, so every failure
  mode closes rather than opens. Judging by ancestry rather than "equals
  the advertised tip" keeps a fetch working when the view ref moves
  between advertisement and POST.
- A refusal is HTTP 200 plus one `ERR` pkt-line, the same shape
  upload-pack uses, so git reports a remote error. "Not in your view" and
  "does not exist" share one message, so the response reveals nothing
  about what the repository holds (requirement 2.3). Refusals are logged.

Only the bounded head is ever buffered (183-345 bytes for a real clone,
shallow clone and incremental fetch; 64 KiB hard cap), so requirement 5.3
still holds.

Evidence: the new integ case in clone-e2e reproduced the leak against a
real vault-manager first (a pack came back for another namespace's page
body), and passes now. Full clone, shallow clone, incremental fetch, an
ancestor commit and clone-during-gc all still pass. Malformed bodies and
protocol v2 bodies are refused rather than guessed at.

Residual limits, recorded in 追補 A: partial-clone lazy fetch asks for
blobs directly and is now refused, so enabling uploadpack.allowFilter
(#11595) requires extending this check first; likewise forwarding the
client's Git-Protocol header, since only v0 is parsed.

Requirements 5.6 and 5.7 are added for the new behaviour; the approved
criterion 5.4 is left as it was.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(vault): bound the work a single upload-pack request can demand

The want check spawns a git process per want, and the client decides how
many wants to send. A 64 KiB want section holds ~1300 want lines, and the
first version answered them with Promise.all: one cheap request measured
1300 concurrent git processes and 1.3 s of churn. Collapse duplicate
OIDs, refuse a request that asks about more than 64 distinct OIDs without
checking any of them, and run the remaining checks one at a time.

Measured after: a normal clone costs one process and 5 ms; 1300 repeats of
one OID collapse to one check (3 ms); 1300 distinct OIDs are refused
without spawning anything; and the worst request still inside the limit
(64 distinct) takes 141 ms with one process at a time.

A view advertises a single commit, and full clone, shallow clone and
incremental fetch were all measured asking for exactly one OID, so 64
leaves ample room.

Also records what the check costs as an installation grows, since that is
the question this raises: 1-2 ms per check against a view holding 20,000
pages with a 1,001-commit chain, unchanged with 5,000 view refs in the
repository. merge-base reads commits only - it opens no tree and no blob -
so page count does not enter into it, user count only affects ref-name
lookup in packed-refs, and squash keeps the commit chain short.

feat(vault): serve partial clone through a published sparse filter

A clone transfers every object in the requester's view. sparse-checkout does
not change that — it only decides what lands in the working tree — and the
history a shallow clone would omit is already squashed away, so the only lever
left is a partial-clone filter.

Of git's filters only `sparse:oid=<blob>` applies the exclusion on the server:
it names a blob of sparse-checkout patterns and upload-pack leaves out the file
bodies they exclude. Measured against a 20,000-page view (15,000 wiki pages,
5,000 under user/): one request, a 252-byte want section, one want, no follow-up
request, and 23.2% less transferred. The want guard added in #11604 accepts that
request unchanged, because it is still a single want for the commit the view
advertises.

`blob:none` is the opposite: it defers every file body for the client to fetch
by object name later, which the guard refuses. `uploadpack.allowFilter` cannot
be enabled for one filter and not another, so those requests are refused before
upload-pack runs, with a message naming the filter that is served. Without that,
`git clone --filter=blob:none` would report "Clone succeeded, but checkout
failed" after a wall of per-object errors and leave an empty working tree —
worse than today's silently-ignored flag.

Only specs the server published are accepted. A `sparse:oid` naming any other
object would let a client learn something from which paths came back.

- vault-sparse-filter.ts (new) — the published specs, their object names, the
  filter decision, and anchoring each spec to a ref so the maintenance gc cannot
  prune it out from under the object name the README publishes
- vault-pkt-line.ts / vault-want-guard.ts — collect `filter` lines from the want
  section alongside the wants
- git-proxy-controller.ts — refuse an unserved filter before upload-pack runs
- vault-upload-pack-spawner.ts — `uploadpack.allowFilter=true`
- server-runtime.ts — publish the specs at boot

Verified by breaking each part in turn: without `allowFilter` both new
integration tests fail (the filter is silently ignored and the excluded body
arrives anyway); without the filter check the blob:none clone reproduces the
failed checkout. 248 unit tests and 22 integration tests pass.

fix(g2g-transfer): harden transfer receiver against auth bypass and path traversal

Two independent defects in the G2G (GROWI-to-GROWI) transfer receiver, chained
in a reported PoC into unauthenticated arbitrary file write when FILE_UPLOAD=local.

1. Auth bypass on generate-key (and the appSiteUrl gate): `app:installed` was read
   once at router setup (server boot) and captured in a closure variable, so an
   instance that finished installation but had not been restarted kept the stale
   `false` and left `/g2g-transfer/generate-key` unauthenticated. Extract a
   `generateAdminRequiredIfInstalled(isInstalled, adminRequired)` middleware that
   reads the install state live (per request); the route now passes a thunk that
   calls `configManager.getConfig('app:installed')` on each request.

2. Path traversal via attachment metadata: the `/g2g-transfer/attachment` handler
   validated the multipart temp file path (`file.path`) but not `attachmentMap.fileName`,
   which is attacker-controlled and joined into the storage path at the local
   uploader sink (`<publicDir>/uploads/user/<fileName>`). Add a pure
   `validateAttachmentMetadata` that requires fileName to be a plain basename
   (no `/`, `\`, `..`, `.`, or NUL) — legitimate attachment fileNames are flat
   md5+ext, so this rejects `../../evil` without breaking real transfers.

Both changes are covered by co-located unit tests, including a regression guard
that the install state is read live rather than captured at factory-creation time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(file-uploader): guard local storage path against traversal at the sink

Defense-in-depth for the g2g-transfer path traversal: the receive boundary now
rejects unsafe attachment fileNames, but an attacker can still inject an
attachments document with a traversal fileName through the collection-import
endpoint. When such an attachment is later delivered, the local uploader would
resolve `<publicDir>/uploads/user/../../<path>` and read a file outside the
uploads root.

Extract `buildLocalStoragePath(basePath, dirName, fileName)`, which joins the
path and throws if it escapes the uploads base, and route the local uploader's
`getFilePathOnStorage` through it. This covers every operation that derives its
path there (upload, delivery, delete, respond), closing the read/delete vector
as well as the write. Legitimate fileNames (flat md5 + extension) always stay
within the base, so real attachments are unaffected. Unit-tested in
local-storage-path.spec.ts.

fix(openapi): resolve APP_PATH before passing it to node --import

`node --import` resolves its value as an ES module specifier, not as a
filesystem path. growi-docs' `api:build` runs this script with

argv path (ts-node, the bundled dist/cli.mjs, `npx tsx`), which resolves
against the cwd in any relative form; the regression came from the same

The asset route answered on every deployment, including those left on draw.io's own hosted

fix(drawio): enforce the asset subtree where the request is made

CodeQL kept flagging the asset fetch as server-side request forgery. The subtree check was
there, but it sat in the function that built the location rather than in the one that reads
it, so nothing about the read itself established the guarantee -- and an analyser has no way
to know a caller upstream did the work.

resolveAsset() now hands back the subtree alongside the location, and readAsset() re-states
the check immediately before fetch. That is the honest place for it: the location is built
from a path the client chose, so "reads nothing outside the subtree it was given" is a
property of the request, not of one call path leading to it. A test covers it by pointing a
read at a live server outside the declared subtree and asserting no request is made.

fix(drawio): fix the asset host by construction rather than by checking it

`new URL(assetPath, subtree)` reads an authority out of the path when there is one, so a
path of `//elsewhere/x` or `http://elsewhere/x` moved the request to another host and was
caught only by the containment check afterwards. Assigning `target.pathname` instead leaves
the origin alone: the host is never parsed from the request-supplied value, so no value of it
can move the request, and such a path just becomes odd-looking path text on the configured
instance. Containment is still checked, because the path setter resolves `..` segments.

Checking a host is weaker than never reading one, and that is the difference CodeQL was
pointing at.

The coverage audit in task 1.2 found seven behaviours with no automated guard and
recorded them as future work. Bringing them into this spec instead: adding a test
does not change behaviour, so it fits inside the as-built boundary, and leaving
known gaps in a document whose purpose is honesty about coverage is the wrong

Requirement 11 states the nine things the new tests must catch, and tasks 4.1-4.5
carry them: the asset router's responses (including that no outbound request is
made when the path is refused), the fetch limits, the four untested postMessage
branches, the load-after entry point, and a drift guard for the self-hosted
judgement.

Two design notes worth keeping:

- The router tests must record whether the upstream fixture was contacted at all.
  Asserting only "404 came back" cannot distinguish a refusal from a request that
  went out and 404-ed there, and "no outbound request" is the actual promise.
- Counting call sites does not guard the single-judgement invariant, since a
  second implementation added elsewhere leaves the count unchanged. The drift spec
  scans for comparisons against the default origin outside the two files allowed
  to make them, and must be mutation-checked before it is trusted.

Requirement 11.6 permits deferring the size limit: a 64 MiB response costs more in
runtime than the guard is worth, and no production seam may be added for it.

test(drawio): Cover the size cap, defer the time cap with the measured reason

Task 4.2, and the record sweep the four earlier tasks left behind.

The size cap is covered by a pair, not a single test. "Refuses a body past the
cap" alone stays green if someone *lowers* the cap, and that is the failure the
production comment actually warns about: a cap under stencils/aws4.xml's 6.5 MB
makes shapes stop rendering with nothing to show why. The second test sends a body
the size of the largest library draw.io ships, so the cap is pinned from both
sides -- verified by raising it to 128 MiB, deleting the check, and lowering it to
1 MiB, each failing the intended test. Cost is ~155 ms.

The time cap is deferred, and the reason is measured rather than assumed: vitest's
fake timers do not drive AbortSignal.timeout. Advancing ten times past the limit
leaves signal.aborted false, because Node schedules it off node:timers rather than
globalThis, and bridging that inside the vitest runtime is never entered. What
remains is a real ten-second wait (measured 10,006 ms), which would take this file
from 0.47 s to ~10.5 s and need a per-test timeout that copies the limit's own
value. Spying on AbortSignal.timeout would assert the mechanism instead of the
limit. Requirement 11.6 permits this trade and forbids adding a production seam for
it, so the finding is recorded in 将来課題 instead.

Also swept the design.md rows the earlier tasks could not touch from inside their
boundaries: the coverage tables now name what 4.1-4.5 added, and the six
"no test exists" rows that are no longer true are gone. What is still unguarded is
down to browser-level rendering, draw.io's own behaviour, and the time cap.

docs(drawio): Make the spec the starting point for changes, not a record

The spec framed itself as a record of an implementation that already existed --
"the behaviour does not change", "not one line of production code was touched",
Non-Goals listing "changing behaviour" as out of scope. That reads as a ledger and
leaves no room for the ordinary case: a small spec change lands, and the
implementation follows it.

Reframed around that case. design.md now opens with what the document is for and
carries a "changing the spec" procedure: fix this document, check the change is not
one of the forms already ruled out, update the acceptance criteria, then the code,
then re-verify. Boundary Commitments own the behaviour rather than the description
of it. Requirement 9 gained an acceptance criterion for the procedure itself.

Also cut it roughly in half, on the principle that anything more reliably learned
by reading the implementation does not belong here: signatures, the file tree, the
requirement traceability table, the Technology Stack, the per-test coverage
enumeration, and the mechanics in Data Models and Error Handling are gone. What is
left is what took real research -- the two forms that cannot be fixed after the
bundle evaluates, why the two entry points exist, why touching window.MathJax is
safe, when the asset route is needed and when it is not -- plus the reasons behind
choices that do not read as obvious from the code, and the refuted theories.

Per-requirement coverage blocks became a single "not guaranteed" line each. Listing
what *is* covered duplicated the spec files and would rot; what cannot be caught by
an automated test is the part a reader cannot derive.

research.md dropped its one-off evidence tables and settled process notes, keeping
how each fact was established and the measurements worth reusing.

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): keep the transfer key alive for the whole receive request

A transfer key dies 30 minutes after its last touch, and one receive request can take
longer than that on its own: the archive arrives over the network, is unzipped, checked,
compared against the existing data, imported collection by collection, and finally
triggers the v5 page normalization — all before the response is written. When the key
runs out in the middle, the destination is left with a replaced database and not one
attachment, because the pusher sends those with the same key afterwards.

The extension therefore starts right after the key is validated, not around the import:
everything before the import handles the same volume of data and can exhaust the key on
its own, and starting in the middleware keeps transfer keys out of ImportService.

It stops on the response's close rather than finish. finish never fires for a client
that disconnects mid-upload, and an extension nobody stops would keep the key alive for
good — the opposite failure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): keep the destination's key alive while the archive is built

Exporting every collection and zipping the result is one uninterrupted stretch during
which the destination is never contacted, and it handles the same volume of data as the
import — so a transfer big enough for the import to outlast the key is one where the
export does too. Nothing has reached the destination yet at that point, so what is lost
is the whole transfer rather than the tail of it.

The source therefore posts to a new keep-alive endpoint at a fixed interval until the
archive is ready. It does not poll growi-info: answering that one writes a probe file to
the destination's attachment storage that nothing deletes, so polling it would litter
the destination for the length of every export.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): put the maintenance mode flag back after importing configs

The flag is a row of the configs collection, and that collection is always imported by
replacement, so importing it deletes the very thing keeping ordinary users out while the
import runs. GROWI already required maintenance mode before a manual zip import and then
dropped it halfway through; the same hole is what a transfer would fall into.

The value written back is the destination's own, read before the import starts, not a
fixed true. Forcing it on would put a destination that was serving normally into
maintenance mode with nobody expecting to switch it off, because the receiving side only
cleans up a flag it raised itself.

It runs in a finally chained onto the configs import, so it also covers a pipeline that
fails after deleteMany has emptied the collection, and it completes before the
loadConfigs() at the end of the import.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): report which collections an import failed to read

The import carries on past a collection it could not read — unchanged policy — but kept
that to itself, so a caller could not tell a completed transfer from one that left the
destination half filled. It now returns the names.

Carrying on turned out not to be what the code actually did. `for await` over an array
of promises awaits each element at the loop head, so a rejection was thrown there rather
than reaching the catch inside the loop body: the first failing collection aborted the
whole import and the catch was unreachable. Replacing it with a plain loop restores the
behaviour that catch was written for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): refuse an import while another one is running

Two imports share one directory of extracted JSON files and one database, so the second
overwrites what the first is about to read and empties collections underneath it. The
window is wider than the import itself: the receive route unzips, re-reads the archive
and queries the destination for conflicts first, which on a large transfer takes minutes.

One claim on ImportService covers it, and both entry points take it before they write
anything into the shared directory. The admin zip import needs it most: its own gate
refuses to run outside maintenance mode, and a transfer puts the destination into
maintenance mode — so during exactly the window that must be protected, that gate waves
an operator's zip straight through.

The receive route releases on the response's close rather than in the handler. multer
aborts the request outright for a non-zip upload or a dropped connection, and the handler
never runs; a claim nobody released would refuse every later import for the life of the
process, reached most easily by a connection dropped mid-transfer — exactly when the
operator retries. The admin route responds before it starts working, so it keeps a
try/finally instead.

The received archive is also stored under a name of our own now: the pusher builds the
uploaded name from the site title and a timestamp it never evaluates, so two sources
named GROWI wrote to the same path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): tell the source operator when the destination only half imported

The two GROWIs are separate processes and the progress notifications come from the
source, which cannot see what happened on the destination. The destination's response to
the archive is the only path that fact can take, and the source was not reading it — so a
transfer that left half the collections behind was announced as complete, and the
operator found out later from the pages that were missing.

The receive route now puts the failed collection names in the response body, the source
reads them, and a non-empty list is reported as a failure naming the collections rather
than as a completion.

The attachments are not sent in that case: the destination holds a partly imported
database and has to be transferred again, so filling it with files now only makes the
retry slower. Requirement 5.2 asks for the attachments to follow a *completed* import.

Also settles each collection's promise where the import starts rather than in the
awaiting loop. Every collection runs at once, so one failing while an earlier one was
still going was a rejection with nothing attached to it — which Node exits the process
over by default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): do not abort a transfer over a collection being replaced

The conflict gate exists because an import that adds to the destination silently drops
the documents that violate a unique index, leaving group-granted pages pointing at users
that were never created (#10151). A collection imported by replacement has none of that:
every existing document is deleted before the archive's are written, so nothing is left
to collide with — and refusing there blocks exactly the case replacement was chosen for,
a destination that already has an admin and a group under the source's names.

Which collections an import replaces is derived from the import settings that arrived,
not from the name of a transfer mode: the destination is never told which mode the
operator picked, and a new mode must not mean teaching this side about it.

A transfer that replaces nothing still aborts on the same collision.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): isolate the collection-wiping tests by database name, not by worker

Running the whole suite showed the dedicated fork was the wrong mechanism: with
`singleFork` every file in the project shares one worker, and the mongo setup's per-file
teardown stops the in-memory server that the next file then tries to connect to. The
project now differs from app-integration only in which files it takes and in
`testDbNamespace`, which is what actually keeps these files off any other project's
database.

Also:
- detect-unique-conflicts.integ.ts loads the configs before importing. The import reads
  the destination's maintenance-mode flag before it starts now, so the configs the server
  loads at boot have to be in place there too.
- the keep-alive tests wait for an extension request that was already on its way before
  taking the baseline they compare against, which was flaky under a full-suite load.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): leave the destination in maintenance mode after importing configs

Importing configs replaces every setting this GROWI has with the archive's, and takes
the flag that keeps ordinary users out with it. What was left behind ran on someone
else's settings and, for a transfer, had not received a single attachment yet — and
whether it was open depended on what the archive happened to carry.

The import now closes it unconditionally and nothing reopens it; the operator is told
beforehand that they will have to switch maintenance mode off themselves (the screens
for that follow in the next commit). This deliberately changes merge-mode behaviour, so
requirement 6.1 now carries the exception and the spec says why.

Also wires the app-integration-exclusive project into `test:integ`. Without it the
project existed but CI never ran it: `test:integ` names `--project=app-integration`
only, and these files had just been excluded from that project — so the two fixes they
guard were verified nowhere. Confirmed by deleting the production code and watching
app-integration stay green.

feat(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): warn before an import or transfer that maintenance mode will stay on

Importing configs now leaves GROWI closed on purpose and nothing reopens it, so the
operator has to be told before they start — afterwards is too late, and for a transfer
the GROWI that closed may not even be the one they are looking at.

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): tie the import claim to the work, and delete the received archive

The claim was released on the response's close. Express does not stop the handler when
the client disconnects, so a transfer whose connection dropped released the claim while
it was still writing — and the retry the operator then makes, or an admin zip import,
could empty a collection underneath it. Releasing on close was still half right: multer
aborts the request outright for a non-zip upload or a dropped upload, and the handler
never runs, so a claim released only there would be held for the life of the process.

The claim now goes into a map keyed by the request; whoever takes it out owns releasing
it. The handler takes it at its start and releases when its work is done; the close
handler only releases what the handler never took. A test that pinned the old behaviour
(the next transfer being accepted while an abandoned one was still importing) now
asserts the opposite.

The received archive is deleted in the same place. Making its name unique removed the
accidental cleanup the constant name used to provide, so a wiki transferred twice left
two full copies on the destination and nothing ever removed them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): stop reporting a partly failed admin import as a success

An import carries on past a collection it cannot read — that is deliberate — but it used
to reject anyway, by accident, and the admin screen turned that rejection into a red
toast. Reporting the failures in the return value instead removed the accident and
nothing replaced it: a zip import that skipped a collection ended with a green
"Import process has completed." and a clean audit row, right before the operator decides
whether to open the wiki again.

The completion event is now withheld when any collection failed, and the executor reports
the names instead and records no success activity. Withholding the event rather than
adding a second one is what avoids a green toast followed by a red one — the screen turns
the completion event into a success unconditionally. A partly failed import leaves no
audit row at all, as it did before this PR; there is no action for it, and adding one
reaches past this change.

Two more things the review found in this path:
- The completion signal fired before loadConfigs() and normalizeAllPublicPages(), while
  the route still held the claim. On a large wiki the screen said "completed" for minutes
  while a retry was answered with 409. It now fires when the work is actually over, from
  a finally so a throw cannot leave the screen importing forever.
- The claim was taken before reading res.locals.activity, which add-activity may never
  set — a throw there kept the claim for the life of the process. The read moved ahead of
  the claim and the audit id is now optional: the import is what the operator asked for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): send the attachments even when some collections failed

The source used to report the failure and return without transferring a single
attachment, leaving the destination with the collections that worked and none of its
files. Requirement 5.2 exists so the attachments are not lost; a partly imported
destination is a worse place to lose them, not a better one.

The mongo state is fixed at ERROR as soon as the import result is known and never
restated as COMPLETED, so the admin screen — which announces success only when both
halves report COMPLETED — cannot call a transfer that lost collections a success. The
failure toast comes after the attachments rather than before, because the screen hides
the progress panel when it arrives and the attachment phase is the long one. A failure
during the attachment transfer is reported on top of, not instead of, the import failure:
only the latter names the collections.

Also maps protected_collection_included, which had no push-side entry and so degraded to
the generic "failed to send the archive" — hiding the one thing that answer carries, the
names of the collections the destination refused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer-migration-mode): fail the configs import when maintenance mode cannot be raised

The write that closes GROWI after importing configs was swallowing its own errors, so a
run whose flag write failed was still reported as a clean success. What that leaves is
the exact state requirement 2.9 exists to prevent: a GROWI running on the archive's
settings, open to users, with (for a transfer) no attachments delivered yet. Letting it
throw marks configs as a failed collection, which is already wired all the way through
to the operator.

Also closes the last gap between claiming the import job and the finally that returns it
(the response was sent in between, and a throw there would have held the claim for the
life of the process), and takes the busy-import error code from the one declaration
instead of repeating the string.

Spec: records that isolating the collection-wiping tests by worker did not work and that
the isolation is by database name, notes on task 9.3 that its maintenance-mode clean-up
predates requirement 2.9, and adds the missing 6.1 to the phase-1 coverage list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer): Check the received archive is inside the import directory before deleting it

CodeQL flags the path handed to rm as user-provided. It reaches multer from the request,
and multer's storage configuration — which composes the stored name from a UUID and the
extension, never from what the caller sent — is not something the analysis can see
through.

Guarded rather than annotated away: this is a delete, so being wrong once costs a file
somewhere else on disk. It is the same check the attachment route already applies before
reading an uploaded file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(g2g-transfer): Deliver the "another import is running" refusal to the source

The receive route decides the refusal from the request headers, before multer
has read the archive. Answered there, it does not reach the source at all: the
connection breaks under the unread upload and the pusher gets a send error in
place of `import_already_in_progress`, leaving the operator with a transfer that
failed for no stated reason. Read the archive to the end and throw it away
before answering.

This is also what made g2g-transfer-import-concurrency.integ.ts fail
intermittently in CI with `write EPIPE`.
